items.title: Take out their five best gameweeks
items.caption:
Someone wins your mini-league every year, and every year they explain why. Here's the test that finds out whether they were any good: take their five best gameweeks out.

I ran it on the model I built. 35% a year became 17%. An index tracker does about 15%. Five trades out of 89 were doing three quarters of the work — which means six years of effort beat doing nothing by two points a year.

Built something yourself? Delete your five best trades and run it again. If the edge disappears, it was never an edge. On 8 October mine stops being a backtest.

run on historical data with paper money — no real positions, past or

items.title: It's like picking your teams in May
items.caption:
I picked my stocks the way you'd cheat at fantasy football: with the final table already in front of me. Took six years to notice, and it wasn't the rules that were wrong.

The rules were clean — nothing peeked at tomorrow. The bias got in when I typed out the list of companies the model is allowed to look at, because I wrote that list this year, knowing which ones had already run.

So ask where your own list came from. If you chose it knowing how the story ended, your backtest is a memory, not a test. On 8 October mine stops being a backtest.

items.title: Deleting the winners didn't reduce the pain
items.caption:
I deleted my five best results. The return halved. The worst run didn't move: −51.3% became −50.9%. The pain was never coming from the trades that worked.

That's the bit people skip. Your winners set the reward; they do almost nothing about the drop. At the worst point half the money was gone and it stayed gone for months before it came back.

So don't judge a system on its good months. Ask what its worst run was, and whether you'd have sat through it. On 8 October I find out whether I can.

items.title: I don't have a fund manager. I wrote one.
items.caption:
I'm an engineer. Not finance. My savings sat in an index tracker doing ten or fifteen percent in a good year, and every so often something would double in a fortnight and I'd read about it on my lunch break.

I could hand it to someone who gets paid whether I win or lose, or I could write down my own rules. So I wrote a runbook: rules, not hunches, trading while I'm at work. Six seasons on paper, 35% a year. Then I went looking for the flaws and found three — they're the next three videos.

On 8 October it stops being paper. Every pick it makes goes up here four weeks later: wins, losses, red arrows. I've no idea how it ends, which is rather the point.
